📘 CHAPTER 7 – WRITING ROUTINE AND POSITIVE MESSAGES

1. Three Parts of a Routine Request (Direct Approach)

PartWhat to include
OpeningClear statement of the request (main idea first)
BodyDetails, justification, benefits to reader (if any)
CloseSpecific action requested, deadline, contact info, thanks

Key tips for opening:

  • Pay attention to tone – use please, I would appreciate
  • Assume compliance – don’t over-convince
  • Be specific – say exactly what you want

Body:

  • Explain smoothly and logically
  • Ask most important questions first
  • Break complex requests into separate questions

Close:

  • Request specific action with deadline (if appropriate)
  • Provide contact information
  • Sincere appreciation

2. Three Common Types of Routine Requests

TypeDescription
Asking for information or actionSimple requests: what you want, why, and benefit to reader
Asking for recommendationsAlways ask permission first; remind who you are; provide details, deadline, and stamped envelope for print
Making claims & requesting adjustmentsOpen calmly with problem; body = full details + proof (invoices, receipts); close = specific action requested; stay professional

3. Strategy for Routine Replies & Positive Messages

Goals:

  • Communicate good news / information
  • Answer all questions
  • Provide all details
  • Leave a good impression

Structure (Direct Approach):

PartContent
OpeningMain idea / good news (clear and concise)
BodyNecessary details, supportive tone; include resale (positive comments about purchase) if appropriate
CloseCourteous, often simple "thank you"; identify follow-up if needed

4. Seven Types of Routine Replies & Positive Messages

  1. Answers to requests for information/action – prompt, gracious, thorough; encourage future sales if applicable
  2. Grants of claims & adjustments – acknowledge, sympathize, take responsibility, explain resolution, repair relationship, follow up
  3. Recommendations – check company policy; include full name, position, relationship, facts/evidence, comparison to peers, overall evaluation
  4. Routine information (updates, policies) – state purpose, give details, highlight benefits if reader may react negatively
  5. Writing instructions – know audience knowledge, give overview, define terms, break into single-task steps, tell expected outcome, test on target user, provide help option
  6. Good news announcements – direct approach; can be press releases (traditional for media, or social media releases with links/quotes)
  7. Goodwill messages – congratulations (achievements, personal milestones), appreciation (recognize contributions), condolences (brief, sincere)

📕 CHAPTER 8 – WRITING NEGATIVE MESSAGES

1. Five Goals of Negative Communication

  1. Convey the bad news
  2. Gain acceptance of the bad news
  3. Maintain as much goodwill as possible
  4. Maintain a good image for your organization
  5. Reduce or eliminate future correspondence on the matter

2. Direct vs. Indirect Approach for Negative Messages

ApproachStructureWhen to use
DirectBad news → Reasons → Positive closeEmergency, routine refusal, recipient prefers direct, minor/routine news
IndirectBuffer → Reasons → Bad news → Respectful closeNews is a shock, reader emotionally invested, high stakes, unexpected

Buffer (indirect opening) – neutral statement that:

  • Expresses appreciation
  • Assures attention to request
  • Shows understanding of reader’s needs
  • Must be relevant and sincere

Bad buffers to avoid:

  • Fake compliments
  • Unrelated details
  • Misleading good news

3. How to Apologize Effectively (4 decisions)

  1. Who – match the person to the severity (CEO for major issues, not for small delays)
  2. Real – no conditional "if" ("I'm sorry if anyone was offended" ❌)
  3. Quick – especially in social media age
  4. Right channel – private conversation, written message, or press conference as appropriate

4. Closing Negative Messages (Both Approaches)

  • Offer alternatives if possible
  • Avoid false hope / false positive endings
  • Describe actions taken to avoid future mistakes (sincere apology signal)
  • Avoid uncertain endings ("I trust our decision is satisfactory" – implies negotiable)
  • Manage future contact (invite follow-up only if open)
  • Be sincere, not cliché

5. Ethics & Etiquette in Negative Messages

  • Laws may require specific disclosure of bad news (finance, safety, environment)
  • Bad news affects lives → be careful and sensitive
  • Don't delay or hide bad news (can be illegal)
  • Whistle-blowing – reporting wrongdoing internally or externally; companies should protect whistleblowers

6. Routine Negative Messages

SituationBest ApproachKey points
Refusing routine requestsDirect (usually)Say no clearly, offer alternatives if possible, don't leave door open ("let me think about it")
Negative announcements (policy changes, ending supplier relationships)Indirect (except minor changes)Buffer → reasons → announcement → positive close
Rejecting suggestions/proposalsIndirect if solicitedExplain fully, especially for employees
Bad news about transactions (delays, etc.)Direct or indirect depending on severityApologize appropriately, explain fix, offer discount/free merchandise to repair relationship
Refusing claims/adjustmentsIndirect (customer emotional)Don't blame or accuse, don't antagonize, respond quickly, be professional

7. Negative Organizational News

Normal circumstances:

  • Match approach to situation
  • Consider unique needs of each audience group
  • Give each audience time to react
  • Plan and manage response
  • Look for positive angles
  • Seek expert advice

Social media environment (rumors, criticism):

  1. Engage early, engage often
  2. Monitor the conversation
  3. Evaluate negative messages
  4. Respond appropriately

Crisis communication (accidents, scandals):

  • Have a crisis management plan (procedures, roles, spokespeople, contact details, media strategy)
  • Respond promptly with accurate information

8. Negative Employment Messages

Refusing recommendation requests – options:

  • Disqualify yourself ("I'm not the best person")
  • Suggest an alternative
  • Take a mentoring approach (explain why not a good fit, offer guidance)
  • Explain personal policy ("I don't provide recommendations")

Refusing social networking recommendation requests – options:

  • Ignore/delete
  • Refrain from making any recommendations
  • Respond to the request

Rejecting job applications:

  • Personalize with name
  • Thank them for applying
  • Use passive voice ("Your application was not selected")
  • Never explain why (legal risk)
  • Don't suggest future reconsideration
  • End with positive wish for future success

Negative performance reviews:

  • Document performance problems
  • Evaluate all employees consistently
  • Write in calm, objective voice
  • Focus on opportunities for improvement
  • Keep job descriptions up to date

Terminating employment:

  • Clearly explain reasons (performance or business-driven)
  • Present reasons fairly
  • Follow company policies, contracts, laws
  • Avoid personal attacks or insults
  • Have another manager review
  • Deliver in person privately

📙 CHAPTER 9 – WRITING PERSUASIVE MESSAGES

1. Three-Step Writing Process for Persuasive Messages

Step 1: Planning

  • Analyze situation (purpose, audience needs, demographics, psychographics, culture, motivation)
  • Gather information
  • Select media/channels (may need multiple)
  • Organize – usually indirect approach; AIDA model

Step 2: Writing

  • Use positive and polite language
  • Understand cultural differences (high-context vs low-context)
  • Be sensitive to organizational culture
  • Build credibility: simple language, objective evidence, cite sources, common ground, fair arguments, audience's best interests, avoid hard sell

Step 3: Completing

  • Evaluate objectively, don't overestimate credibility
  • Revise for clarity and conciseness
  • Ask colleague to review
  • Proofread meticulously
  • Choose right distribution method

2. Four Essential Strategies for Persuasive Business Messages

#StrategyExplanation
1Frame your argumentsUse AIDA model (Attention, Interest, Desire, Action)
2Balance emotional & logical appealsBusiness relies more on logic, but emotion helps; consider actions, expectations, resistance, your power position
3Reinforce your positionUse evidence, expert quotes, vivid language, metaphors, anecdotes, audience benefits
4Anticipate objectionsAddress concerns early; for hostile audience, present all sides before recommendation

3. The AIDA Model (Very Important)

PhaseWhat to do
AttentionGrab interest – common ground, question, surprise
InterestAdd details, show benefits
DesireExplain how change helps them, answer objections
ActionSpecific request, deadline if applicable

Limitations of AIDA:

  • Talks at audience, not with them
  • Focuses on one-time events, not long-term relationships

4. Emotional vs. Logical Appeals

AppealBased onBusiness use
EmotionalFeelings (freedom, success, comfort)Makes audience receptive, but not enough alone
LogicalFacts, evidence, reasoningPrimary in business – saves money, improves quality

Three types of logical reasoning:

  • Analogy – familiar comparison to explain unfamiliar
  • Induction – specific evidence → general conclusion
  • Deduction – general principle → specific case

Logical fallacies to avoid:

  • Hasty generalizations
  • Circular reasoning
  • Flawed analogies
  • Ad hominem attacks
  • Oversimplification
  • False cause-effect

5. Common Persuasive Mistakes to Avoid

MistakeWhy it's bad
Hard sellPressuring feels self-serving; use soft sell instead
Resisting compromisePersuasion often requires give-and-take
Relying solely on great argumentsNeed emotion and storytelling too
Assuming persuasion is one-shotUsually gradual process

6. Three Categories of Persuasive Business Messages

  1. Persuasive requests for action – use AIDA if unexpected; gain credibility; make action easy
  2. Persuasive ideas – change attitudes/beliefs without immediate action; reexamine opinions
  3. Persuasive claims/adjustments – when normal process fails; start with problem, review actions, be specific, appeal to fairness/goodwill, close respectfully

7. Marketing & Sales Messages

TypeGoal
Marketing messagesGuide buyers through process, no immediate decision, introduce brand
Sales messagesAsk for immediate purchase decision

Planning marketing/sales messages:

  • Assess audience needs
  • Analyze competition
  • Determine key selling points (features) and benefits (user advantages – practical, emotional)
  • Anticipate purchase objections (price, quality, compatibility, risk)

AIDA in sales:

  • Attention: headline, emotional appeal, visual
  • Interest: fulfill headline promise, explain benefits
  • Desire: testimonials, comparisons, demos, guarantees
  • Action: clear, simple, risk-free call to buy

8. Persuasive Messages for Social Media & Mobile

Social media approach:

  • Facilitate community building (Facebook groups, forums)
  • Listen actively
  • Initiate and respond (blogs, newsletters)
  • Provide useful information
  • Support your champions (loyal customers)
  • Be authentic, conversational
  • Blend traditional marketing (AIDA where appropriate)

➡️ Shift from promotion to relationship-building

Mobile marketing guidelines:

  • Keep messages short and simple
  • Ensure fast, easy user experience
  • Mobile used for: product reviews, store locations, coupons/ discounts, price comparisons

9. Ethics, Legal Compliance & Etiquette in Persuasion

Do's:

  • Be truthful and transparent
  • Support claims with reliable evidence
  • Avoid bait-and-switch
  • Protect children (parental consent)
  • Keep promises (marketing messages can be seen as contracts)
  • Respect privacy (opt-in emails only, no unauthorized use of name/image)

Etiquette:

  • Audience-centered approach
  • Opt-in newsletters show "you" attitude
